rv.q: The acting is terrific across the board, but you can probably sense the way Ms. Kennedy has overentangled her characters, like an anxious sailor making redundant knots.
Yet thanks to sensitive performances, Kennedy's mechanics frequently work as designed, cranking up the stakes and delivering vivid emotional moments on cue.
For all its seeming authenticity — the play was inspired by events in the life of the playwright’s mother — the evening feels as ersatz as today’s tourist-clogged Little Italy.

“In ‘Napoli, Brooklyn’ playwright Meghan Kennedy creates the vivid ongoing life of Brooklyn in the 1960s…Shades of Neil Simon’s Brooklyn stories and Arthur Miller’s 'A View from the Bridge' infuse Kennedy’s stinging sense of realism.
Her writing in Napoli, Brooklyn, demonstrates why, revealing a classic probing of the meaning of family, the conflicting dimensions of love and the shadowy influence of fate upon destiny.
Kennedy is more-than-capable of incisive characterizations, smart dialogue, and revealing the depths hidden beneath the surface of these ordinary people.
An excellent cast helps disguise the play’s weaknesses while bringing the roles to vibrant life.

But there just seems to be too much pasta in the pot.
Full of interest, the play is also full of head-scratching anomalies.
But the play overall is suggestive of the title of Ms. Kennedy's previous outing for the Roundabout: Too Much, Too Much, Too Many .

Napoli, Brooklyn is, for much of its running time, a remarkably sluggish drama built around a first-act curtain so shocking that I'm a little surprised it doesn't nightly inspire an audience panic attack.
All in all, Napoli, Brooklyn a satisfying portrait of a very specific group of people living in a time and place that is made clear to us.
Napoli, Brooklyn has the palpable sense of someone’s actual family story.
The second act is a powerhouse of a production in many ways.
This stereotypic drama is also an intimate portrait of the immigrant working-class life, though it seems more like a Hallmark TV movie than a major Off-Broadway play.
The cast does valiantly in this action-packed melodrama that tackles so much—family, marital abuse, immigration, feminism, same-sex love, and unanticipated catastrophe (again, no spoiler).
What's left are stereotypes and platitudes.
Actually the title of her earlier play would have been more suitable for this one because it suffers from too much plot and too many characters.

cn.t: Kennedy's family drama about 1960s Italian immigrants in Brooklyn earns praise for strong performances and vivid atmosphere, but critics find the storytelling familiar and uneven, with an overstuffed plot and jarring tonal shifts.
